arXiv:2610.25985v1 [cs.CR] 19 Oct 2026

NIOCIS: Typed-Decision Next-Hop Routing
with Node-Conditioned Option Spaces
for Tool-Use Agents

Jin Han    Mingfeng Xin Affiliation: Feng Liang    Jingtao Yu Affiliation: Independent Researcher
Abstract

Tool-use agents pay per decision: at each hop a language model re-reads the state and thinks for seconds, though its actions are finite and its decisions recur. We present NIOCIS, a routing layer that folds execution logs into a loop-collapsed action graph—forward action transitions plus explicit recovery back-edges—and answers one typed question: which declared option at a state, plus stop, does the fleet take next? A small model reads a calibrated distribution over them in one pass, generating no text. On 1,615 production security-operations episodes we measure what the layer replaces, returns and is bounded by. It replaces the per-decision deliberation: the typed encoder matches the logged next hop on 32.2% of the 3,875 held-out decisions (34.9% within the declared options) in 10 ms of encoder time (19.5 ms for the typed-choice form), against 2.2 s per LLM hop; two feature readouts on the same decisions reach 32.8% and 32.3%, an ordering the paired test does not resolve, so the typed layer is chosen for cost rather than for a separated accuracy lead. Tuning moves a language model: jpt-4b reaches 9.9% zero-shot and 31.9% fine-tuned, a gap an exact paired test does not resolve (p=0.68p=0.68), at 244 ms per decision. It returns little: the realised hop falls outside the declared options for 7.9% of decisions and outside the model’s top twenty for 9.3%, while the most confident 15% holds 91.9% accuracy, a band three different confidence rules trace alike. And it is bounded: the state text binds accuracy, not the candidate count, the deliberation budget or the parameter count; node discovery saturates at the rate a zero-parameter occupancy null predicts, and on five public process logs a variable-order Markov table collects most of each margin over the majority baseline; a cross-trace leave-one-out test puts the released state’s ceiling at 25.6–44.9% as the state key grows more specific, repeated states disagreeing more often than they agree; and the option-space ablation attributes the gain to per-node candidate restriction (+3.5 points over a flat catalog) rather than graph traversal (zero within its interval). The claim is narrow: containment and a small high-precision band at millisecond cost; a gated self-evolution loop lifts every arm above its anchor yet ends below full supervision; a confidence-gated cascade loses agreement when the escalation arm is the zero-shot stand-in rather than the tuned model; and agreement past a third of the fleet needs a state carrying the plan and the observation, which the released records do not.

1 Introduction

LLM agents that call tools decide by inference. At every step of every task the model re-derives what it already decided last week for the same tool in the same situation: whether to search before reading, whether to write directly or route through approval, whether to retry or roll back. The latency of such a judgment is counted in seconds and its cost in thinking tokens (Cheng et al., 2026; Li et al., 2026a), even though the decision’s support is small—a closed set of declared next actions, median 46 per state here—and the deployment’s accumulated logs already contain the answer, thousands of times over.

Three observations motivate NIOCIS. Execution logs converge. An internal deployment’s tools and action semantics are finite; as episodes accumulate, the action vocabulary saturates while the logs keep growing. Process mining has exploited this regularity for business event logs for two decades (van der Aalst, 2016; Leemans et al., 2013), and recent results compress agent-trace corpora into finite-state machines of 7–43 states (Cho et al., 2026); the complexity-vs-log-size reading we cite tracks only the state-count curve (§2). Also, typed decisions can be cheap. A decision model that answers exactly one of its caller’s declared options—reading a calibrated distribution from a single forward pass, with no generated text—decides in 30–65 ms (Cheng et al., 2026; Ren et al., 2026) at accuracy within a few points of LLM judges (Ren et al., 2026), and works as a first-tier agent decision layer that escalates on low confidence (Wu & Lim, 2026; Li et al., 2026c). And logs can train their own router: routing decisions, executions and outcomes form a data flywheel (Liu et al., 2026; NeoHorse Team et al., 2026), provided the update loop is gated against collapse (Nguyen et al., 2026b; Shang et al., 2026).

NIOCIS composes these into one loop (Figure 1): (i) we induce a loop-collapsed action graph from episode logs—a directed graph of forward action transitions (self-loops aside) with recovery back-edges carrying rollbacks, backtracks and task redirects; (ii) we route with the typed-decision router whose option set is exactly the current node’s outgoing edges (plus stop), whose output is a calibrated distribution the caller can threshold, and whose uncertain cases escalate to the LLM; (iii) we self-evolve: each real episode becomes training data, updates pass a rollback gate and survive only with evidence, and any update that regresses beyond the gate tolerance (δ\delta) is rolled back. In the full design, executed episodes are budget-bounded (a step budget and a per-node revisit cap; §3). Our contributions are:

  • •

    P1 The loop-collapsed action graph. We formalize induction from episode logs with explicit folding rules for loops and back-edges, and quantify the growth of the induced action graph (E1): transition discovery shows diminishing returns and loop-event rates reach a stable regime, while node-vocabulary convergence is not offered as an independent finding—a zero-parameter occupancy null already predicts it (§6).

  • •

    P2 Typed-decision path routing. We define next-hop selection as a typed decision over a node-conditioned declared option space (the current node’s outgoing edges, plus stop) and implement it with one-pass feature-MLP readouts that reach 32.8% agreement with the deployed fleet’s own choices (35.6% within the declared space; the hidden-state probe variant gives up two points of masked accuracy and decodes from its 10 ms encoder pass, the typed family’s full predict running 19.5 ms p50), together with an accept/escalate gate analyzed with risk–coverage curves (E2); a transition-table baseline over all nine decision streams (App. B) reaches 31.1% on SOC. We also measure what the restriction is worth (E9): the node-conditioned space beats a flat 155-class catalog by 3.5 points and a size-matched global-frequency space by 1.4 points, but is statistically indistinguishable from a node-conditioned space built without graph traversal, so we claim the per-node restriction, not graph traversal. We therefore claim the formalization and the measurement rather than the traversal: the contribution is to define the next-hop choice as a typed decision over a node-conditioned declared option space, and to bound what that construction can reach on production logs, which Section 7 does quantitatively.

  • •

    P3 A gated self-evolution loop, with route replay as a measurement. We replay held-out episodes against a re-prompted MIMO Pro V2.6 stand-in (one reasoning call per hop for the fleet’s LLM component: no per-stage orchestration, no tool results; §5); the route view renders the per-decision quantities—strict survival, plus a wrong-hop cost rescaling of the mismatch count—so we report it as a measurement on that graph (§6), and add the one route quantity that is not such a rescaling—the first-divergence hop index and type (median hop 2, most first divergences on escalated hops)—reading the replay as placing the cheap readout in the agreement/cost corner and the accept/escalate hybrid between its parents (the readout and the opponent; E3); and we exercise a self-evolution loop whose rollback gate scores every candidate while the loop absorbs a 12%-of-one-batch label-corruption stress, the gate refusing 13 of the 40 candidate updates, in 6 of the 10 seeded chains (E4).

The core experiments (E1–E4) run on real execution logs from a production security-operations agent fleet (§5 states provenance); E5 replicates the constructions on public event logs and open tool-use trajectories, and any Langfuse-style observations export folds into the same episode schema.

2 Related Work

Workflow and skill induction from agent logs.

Agent Workflow Memory (Wang et al., 2024) induces reusable routines from trajectories and feeds them back as context; task-model induction (Jiang et al., 2026) builds hierarchical goal/procedure models from computer-use traces; automata induction compresses trace corpora into compact finite-state machines for next-step prediction and failure detection (Cho et al., 2026); the literature-search agent PaperPilot induces editable search-operator directed acyclic graphs (DAGs) (Li et al., 2026b). Skill-graph systems organize experience for retrieval: HiSkill’s hierarchical skill graphs (Hao et al., 2026), SE-GoS’s self-evolving graph-of-skills (Fu et al., 2026), CaSKG’s counterfactual-causal skill graphs (Li et al., 2026d), GraphSkillAA’s validated skill-graph updates (Shang et al., 2026), GraphSkillEvo’s evolutionary graph skills (Sun et al., 2026a), and skill distillation from browsing traces (Yang et al., 2026). M2-PALE applies process mining to agent traces for explanation (Qian et al., 2026); AgentHER recycles trajectories into training data (Ding, 2026). Every workflow and skill system surveyed here uses the induced structure for retrieval, prompting, explanation or training (the automata-induction uses of the same structure are treated next). Automata-based next-step prediction and failure detection over induced machines (Cho et al., 2026) are the closest runtime uses: both score a fixed label vocabulary from trace prefixes (held-out scoring offline against the induced machine; its failure ranker also runs as an online monitor over partial traces) rather than binding the induced graph’s edges as declared options. Interleaved reason-and-act control loops keep an LLM in the loop at every step (Yao et al., 2023), self-reflective retry feeds verbal feedback back into the next attempt (Shinn et al., 2023), and open-ended agents grow executable skill libraries as text (Wang et al., 2023); we instead bind the induced graph as the decision space of a single-pass readout, with no per-step LLM call. None of the surveyed systems makes the induced graph the runtime decision space of a millisecond-scale model, and none reports route-level divergence accounting (episodic survival and wrong-hop cost) for routes over an induced graph on production agent logs (the accounting scores realized routes, not a model’s conformance fitness van der Aalst, 2016; alignment-based conformance checking instead replays each trace against a discovered model and scores the cheapest replay (Adriansyah et al., 2011; Carmona et al., 2018)). Read as a discovered model the induced graph is a permissive one—on held-out traces, token-level replay fitness 0.910.91, trace-level 0.590.59, escaping-edge precision 0.020.02 (each state enables its whole declared option set), edge-level generalization 0.270.27 (App. B)—which is why our comparison is against option-space constructions, leaving process-discovery models aside. Paul & Nandy (2026) study cost-optimal multi-step model/tool routing (a different decision axis).

Process mining.

Discovery of process models from event logs is a mature field (van der Aalst, 2016); constructive miners capture loop and concurrency structure (Leemans et al., 2013; Kourani et al., 2025), and monotonicity characterizations control candidate-place growth (Tacke genannt Unterberg et al., 2026). The complexity-vs-log-size reading we cite reports stable small automata (7–43 states on public corpora, Cho et al., 2026); it carries no loop-event or transition-pair axis. E1 adds those axes on a production security-operations-center (SOC) corpus, with subsample-median bands, and measures the loop structure directly. A parallel line, predictive process monitoring, answers the next-activity question by scoring a fixed activity vocabulary from prefixes (Tax et al., 2017); its standard n-gram realization is the backoff-Markov baseline of E5 (re-gated here onto the shared declared option sets).

Typed-decision models and LLM routing.

Typed-decision models answer exactly one of their caller’s declared options from a single forward pass, with calibrated probabilities and no generated text: this-that-model-1.0 reads answers from hidden state at 30.9 ms (Cheng et al., 2026); the one-pass judge we label JevLite (small one-pass model of Ren et al. (2026)) reads temperature-scaled answer-label logits at 64.5 ms per decision on one consumer GPU. As judges they accept when confident and escalate when unsure (Li et al., 2026c); as agent control layers they cut strong-model calls 72.7% at 95% task success against a strong-only baseline of 88% on the same frozen benchmark (Wu & Lim, 2026); at the edge they cut decision latency and API fees (Li et al., 2026a), and with an LLM planner they close fast control loops (Ma et al., 2026). Unlike these flat typed-control layers’ static action-list option sets, NIOCIS’s option set is the outgoing edge set of an induced action graph; NIOCIS also performs route-level divergence accounting over that graph, quantifies its node-vocabulary convergence, and exercises a gated self-evolution loop, none of which flat typed-control layers do. Guided or grammar-constrained decoding also restricts an output space, but it filters a generator step by step (Geng et al., 2023); the typed readout instead emits one distribution over the declared options in a single pass. Constrained decision heads are sensitive to option labeling (Sun et al., 2026b), which motivates our edge identifiers. Model/tool routers choose which solver runs (Chen et al., 2023; Ong et al., 2024; Paul & Nandy, 2026; Liu et al., 2026; Bala & Shah, 2026) (or generate retrieval configurations Pan et al., 2026), not which graph edge advances a task; preference-trained small routers have cut cost by over 2×2\times at matched quality in some evaluated settings (Ong et al., 2024); typed artifacts share tool-routing knowledge across agents (Chakraborty et al., 2026); and router infrastructure now spans development, evaluation and deployment, where lightweight routers prove more competitive under tight-cost constraints (Feng et al., 2026), though routing accuracy plateaus below the oracle (Lu et al., 2026). Amortized planning replaces search with direct action inference in world models (Nguyen et al., 2026a); we amortize workflow-path decisions into a declared-option readout over an induced action graph.

Self-evolving agents.

Routing decisions and executions can train their own successors (Liu et al., 2026; NeoHorse Team et al., 2026) as long as the loop is gated: unguarded self-evolution can collapse or suffer security drift (Nguyen et al., 2026b; Li & Zhu, 2026), while validated updates with rollback keep graphs healthy (Shang et al., 2026) and recursive-in-recursive designs keep harness and weights co-evolving (Xue et al., 2026). Our E4 adds a minimal complete instance—accumulate, gate on held-out performance, roll back on regression—and deploys it under label corruption that the gated loop absorbs on average (the refusal path refuses 13 of the 40 candidate updates, in 6 of the 10 seeded chains).

3 Problem Formulation

Episode logs.

A log is a set of episodes. An episode is a sequence of steps e=⟨s1,…,sT⟩e=\langle s_{1},\dots,s_{T}\rangle where each step sts_{t} records an action label L⁡(st)∈𝒱L(s_{t})\in\mathcal{V} (an action semantic such as db.write), a step kind (advance, retry or back: a back step revisits an earlier label, opening a return edge in E−E^{-}) and a context vector 𝐜∈[0,1]d\mathbf{c}\in[0,1]^{d} (full-design schema: urgency, dependencies, authorization, complexity, …). Episodes carry a start, a goal—in the full design a node g∈𝒢⊆𝒱g\in\mathcal{G}\subseteq\mathcal{V}—and an outcome.

Loop-collapsed action graph.

Straight traces understate structure; agents loop. Folding an episode yields a skeleton—retry runs folded as temporally extended steps in the sense of Sutton et al. (1999)—to which the step’s label L⁡(st)L(s_{t}) is appended except in two step kinds: (a) an immediate retry of the last label kept in the skeleton (the retry is dropped), and (b) a revisit of an earlier-visited label (the step is appended as usual and a new kept frame—a skeleton entry—opens at the revisit). Both kinds are recorded as loop events (retry for (a), back for (b)); a retry—which includes every continuation of a same-label run—is the only kind left out of the skeleton. Folding the 22,192 logged tool calls thus drops exactly the 4,124 retries and keeps 15,704 forward advances plus 2,364 recovery returns (18,068 decision states); E1’s event rates reflect this disposition. Observed kept-frame transition pairs (E+∪E−E^{+}\cup E^{-}) over all episodes define the transition volume reported in E1; first-visit forward transfers give E+E^{+} and executed returns to earlier labels give recovery back-edges E−E^{-} (this corpus-census set is computed over all folds and persisted with the corpus for characterization only; the operational option graph is induced from the training fold, §4), while same-label repeats surface only as retry events, as described above. The two roles a pair can play—forward transfer and recovery return—overlap on real traces: of the 2,536 distinct observed pairs, 2,315 appear as first-visit forward transfers and 702 as recovery returns (481 pairs play both roles—forward in one context, return in another—while 221 pairs are exclusively returns; App. A gives the fold breakdown). The loop-collapsed action graph is G=(V,E+∪E−)G=(V,E^{+}\cup E^{-}). The observed forward set is not a DAG: 1,272 of its 2,315 pairs fall into 636 mutual couples (u→vu{\to}v and v→uv{\to}u between nodes uu and vv, both arcs observed as forward transfers), so forward transfers alone carry directed 2-cycles. What planning needs still holds: all edge weights are strictly positive, so an optimal walk to a reachable goal can always be chosen simple (no repeated node), even though execution may loop. Complexity is measurable two ways—folded (semantic nodes and transitions) and occurrence-tagged (per-kind step occurrences)—and loop mass is an occurrence-tagged quantity: the loop-event share of executed steps, 100​(retry+back)/steps100(\mathrm{retry}+\mathrm{back})/\mathrm{steps} (29.2% of the SOC corpus’s steps). Figure 2 draws the same graph one level up: the catalog actions grouped into capability families, with the family-to-family traffic that a station-level view hides.

Next-hop decision problem and route-level criterion.

Let π⁡(a∣v,g,𝐜)\pi(a\mid v,g,\mathbf{c}) be a router at the current node vv over the declared option set A⁡(v)=succ⁡(v)∪{stop}A(v)=\mathrm{succ}(v)\cup\{\texttt{stop}\} (options identified with their edges). The reference next hop is the deployed fleet’s logged choice at the same realized state; the full design substitutes the next hop of a context-weighted shortest-path walk to the goal gg for that logged choice (a guard fact (a,η)(a,\eta) pairs an action aa with a context precondition over slot η\eta, say an authorization level; a failed fact multiplies the cost wew_{e} of the edge labeled aa by a penalty factor γ>1\gamma>1, so a walk whose context is at a low authorization level is routed through an approval detour). Per step we report top-1 agreement with the reference. At the route level we report strict survival—an episode’s fidelity to this one realized reference trace, where survival requires every one of its decisions to match (a trajectory-fidelity reading, separate from any fleet-level safety or availability property)—and the wrong-hop gap, the accumulated cost of diverging hops over the whole teacher-forced episode under per-hop conventions c1=1c_{1}=1 and c3=3c_{3}=3; clipping that accounting at the first divergence would understate the cost of long episodes, so the first-divergence (strict-survival) view and the unclipped wrong-hop gap are reported side by side. Under this teacher-forced accounting the gap is a fixed rescaling of the per-decision mismatch count—(#​decisions/#​episodes)​(1−agreement)(\#\text{decisions}/\#\text{episodes})\,(1-\text{agreement})—so its extra information over per-decision agreement is the episode-length weighting; strict survival is the genuinely route-level measure.

Typed decisions and gated escalation.

The full typed design’s output is a distribution over A⁡(v)A(v) and nothing else: options are structurally identified (stable edge identifiers, never surface names, in the full design), the answer is read from one forward pass (as in Cheng et al., 2026; Ren et al., 2026), and malformed outputs are unrepresentable (the corpus readout emits over the global vocab then masks to A⁡(v)A(v), cf. A3). A confidence gate accepts at threshold τ\tau when maxaπ(a∣⋅)≥τ\max_{a}\pi(a\mid\cdot)\geq\tau and otherwise escalates to the LLM, mirroring accept/judge cascades (Li et al., 2026c; Wu & Lim, 2026). Since a valid output is not a guarantee of progress, the full design runs execution under a step budget BB and a per-node revisit cap RR, terminating the episode (failure) on either violation. The corpus study of §5 instead replays logged episodes teacher-forced and so exercises neither bound.

4 The NIOCIS Approach

4.1 Graph induction and loop folding

Folding follows the two rules of §3; the induction pass book-keeps skeleton transitions and loop events incrementally per episode. Recovery back-edges discovered during execution—rollbacks, backtracks and task redirects—are recorded alongside the corpus; the §5 census over them (E+E^{+}, E−E^{-}) is computed over all folds and is purely descriptive. The operational option graph, by contrast, is induced from the training fold alone and is one shared object: routers and rollouts see the same train-induced option graph at training and at evaluation time, with no held-out edge ever entering the runtime candidate set (see Option supply below). We deliberately do not merge near-synonymous actions—semantic action labels are the unit of decision, matching how typed decisions declare their options (Cheng et al., 2026). Because option surfaces are load-bearing for constrained heads (Sun et al., 2026b), edge options are rendered over stable internal identifiers rather than surface names, in the full design. (Option supply. In the corpus realization the declared option set at vv is the train-split fold’s kept-frame transitions out of vv, first-visit advances and recovery returns alike, plus stop—graph induction and routing share one graph, so the option space carries the induction’s misses, 7.9% of test targets falling outside it—§5; Figure 3a reports the observed-transition volume this induction processes.)

4.2 Typed-decision readout router

We call the model the typed-decision router; its scoring head is the readout. The router answers one question per state: given the current node vv, goal gg and context 𝐜\mathbf{c}, which edge in A⁡(v)A(v) leads to task completion? (A⁡(v)A(v) includes stop as a non-edge option.) In the corpus realization gg is the episode’s agent-stage identity—constant within an episode, hardwired to 0 on the E5 streams—and 𝐜\mathbf{c} is structural (prefix shape, visit counters, per-node neighbor statistics); the guard-aware 𝐜\mathbf{c} of the full design feeds only the substituted context-weighted walk. Options are the declared outgoing edges, bound to stable single-token identifiers: target-action classes over the corpus’s 154-name tool catalog (plus stop) in the class-space readout, or edge identifiers of the induced graph in the edge-ID readout (§6 compares both); in the hidden-state arms the answer distribution is read from the hidden state at a designated position (as in Cheng et al., 2026; Ren et al., 2026)—equivalently, a softmax over the declared label logits (temperature-scaled only in our zero-shot arm)—while the feature arms parameterize the same softmax over observable features (the edge-ID readout space applies to both backbones); nothing is generated. Training minimizes proper-scoring losses over the full vocabulary softmax on (state, goal, context, next-hop) tuples copied from held-in logged transitions—behavioral cloning (Pomerleau, 1991) of the deployed fleet (out-of-space targets stay in the objective; option masking enters only at the masked-renormalized (masked-renorm) gate at decode); the full design replaces the logged next hop with planner-oracle labels—the hop of a context-weighted shortest-path walk to the goal—and uses the walk-membership and episode-success questions as the oracle’s post-hoc reward signal. Calibration is reported as expected calibration error (ECE-15, the 15-bin convention; temperature-fitted Guo et al., 2017 for the zero-shot arm, raw masked-renorm confidence for all trained arms, over the probe and feature backbones and their class-space and edge-ID variants). Plain cross-entropy (CE) and the CE-plus-Brier (CE++Brier) objective (Ren et al., 2026) are compared head-to-head on both readout families: a multilayer perceptron over observable features (the feature MLP; node, goal, context, visit counters, per-node neighbor statistics) and a hidden-state probe on the Laya encoder (421M parameters; essentially the same construction as the designated-position hidden-state readout of Cheng et al. (2026)). Typed decodes of the probe-family heads of Cheng et al. (2026) and Ren et al. (2026) run 30–65 ms at batch-1. Deployment is a two-tier decision stack: the readout handles control decisions (which edge); an executor synthesizes arguments; free-form generation stays in the LLM (as in Wu & Lim, 2026).

4.3 Gated self-evolution (RSI)

We use the term recursive self-improvement (RSI) narrowly for the accumulate–gate–commit loop below, not for weight-space self-modification. Decision states of executed walks are labeled with the reference next hop—alternatively the full design’s planner-oracle labels—and appended to a replay buffer; each round trains a candidate router on the accumulated buffer. An update is committed only if held-out validation performance does not regress beyond δ=0.005\delta=0.005 (half an accuracy point); otherwise the candidate is discarded and the incumbent kept. On the 371–380-row validation-gate fold (380 where the stream split is row-granular; App. A), a 0.5-point bar is about 1.9 rows, comparable to the fold’s own single-row resolution of 0.26–0.27 points; this δ\delta is thus a coarse safety threshold rather than a confidence-interval-backed test. The ten-chain study’s paired gate-score differences make that resolution explicit. Twelve of its 13 refusals regress the gate fold by 3 or more rows; a single 2-row refusal sits exactly at δ\delta’s own granularity (the finest distinction a 380-row gate set can support is one row); and 6 of the 27 accepted updates carry a gate-score dip worth one row that δ\delta accepts by construction. We therefore report the 13/40 refusal count as a coarse operational safety readout, not a high-resolution statistical test of regression (validation-gated update with rollback, cf. Shang et al., 2026; held-out selection as in Nguyen et al., 2026b). E4 exercises the loop under 12% label corruption in one round: on the plotted seed-0 chain the gate score never regresses and no rollback fires there—so the guardrail is deployed and measured; across ten seeded chains its refusal path fires 13 times in 40 attempts (App. A).

5 Experimental Setup

Data provenance (production SOC traces).

All experiments run on real execution logs: a Langfuse observability export of 22,328 records (22,192 tool calls plus 136 generation records) over 1,656 traces from a production SOC agent fleet (September 2026). Keeping the trace-ID groups with at least one tool call yields 1,615 episodes over a 154-name tool catalog with real per-call latencies and four domain slices (detection 1,174, response 245, protection 139, recognition 54; two minor agents pool the remaining 3 episodes). The slice names are the deployment’s own agent-stage labels and are left unmapped to external taxonomies: a slice enters the router as part of its goal input, so we report it under its native name and do not translate it into another vocabulary’s terms. Corpus statistics appear in Table 1. Two properties of the export shape what can be measured and are disclosed up front: tool result payloads and agent chat bodies (where report text lives) are stripped, so the router’s state is reconstructed from the observable call structure—labels and ordering; and task outcomes must be derived. Our derivation: an episode is completed when it closes with the agent’s own close-out act update_goal{status: complete} (present in 1,070 episodes, always within the final two steps of the fold), blocked on status: blocked (5), and abandoned when no close-out occurs (540). The convention is machine-checkable (an LLM judge re-prompted to the convention reproduces it on all 1,615 episodes; because the judge is handed the convention itself, this certifies internal consistency, not independent validity) and the derived labels are weak—convention-derived, not independently annotated—and received a manual re-reading on 30 sampled episodes (23/3/4 across detection/response/protection), adjudicated by an AI assistant from session logs rather than a separate human auditor (the structural rule agrees 30/30; an unconstrained judge prompt expecting report text inside update_goal agrees only 622/1,615, or 38.5%, over the full corpus—a shortfall that measures the export’s missing field rather than task failure: this caution is revisited in §9). Services: the re-prompted E3 opponent is MIMO Pro V2.6 and the labeling judge is DS V4.1 Flash, both production reasoning models behind our serving gateway (vLLM-served Kwon et al., 2023); the typed encoder’s backbone is Laya 0.3.21, an open non-autoregressive typed-decision engine built on the ModernBERT-large encoder (Warner et al., 2025) with a marker-position decision head. Its shipped per-bucket decision temperatures include an out-of-range entry, so the zero-shot arm refits one scalar temperature on validation negative log-likelihood (henceforth NLL; all trained arms report raw masked-renorm confidence). Service and judge latencies are measured in vivo under production load; the zero-shot arm’s 0.30 s p50 is in-vivo CPU runtime (App. B); typed-model timings are batch-1 GPU wall clock (App. B); no latency or judge-error models are used. The one remaining synthetic element is deliberate and scoped: E4’s 12% label corruption is a controlled stress injection (a stand-in for policy regressions), not a claim about the deployment’s noise rate.

Replay protocol (held-out logs as the environment).

The production logs are the environment: held-out episodes are replayed decision-by-decision and every policy faces the same reference behavior—the deployed fleet’s own choices at each realized state. Per decision the policy sees the declared option set (the current label’s outgoing edges in the train-induced graph, plus stop) and a prefix rendering that differs by arm. The feature arm summarizes the folded kept prefix, while the probe and zero-shot state texts render an eight-entry window of the raw label list, cut at the kept frame’s fold ordinal (its rank among kept frames), which serves as the raw-list index. Each entry is rendered by its name tail (the substring after the last __, or the whole entry when it contains none), so distinct catalog actions can collide (two search actions surface identically). The zero-shot arm’s option criteria render the same tails with underscores as spaces, barring the <stop> criterion whose text reads conclude; colliding options then present identical choice texts. The window runs behind the current label by exactly the retries preceding the frame (the retries stay in the list; on such rows the typed arms never see the current label), while the LLM prompt renders the same window with full labels (not name tails) and appends the current label explicitly. Scoring is teacher-forced against the logged next hop; episodes are scored two ways—strict survival (an episode terminates at its first divergence) and the wrong-hop gap accumulated over the whole episode (cost conventions 1 and 3 per wrong hop are both reported throughout). Because the reference is a realized trajectory rather than an oracle, task success inherits the derived outcome labels above, and the declared option space is itself scored: 7.9% of test targets lie outside the train-declared options (declared-space coverage 92.1%, or 91.3% when recovery edges are restricted to states the running prefix has already visited—29 rows, every one of them a return to an unvisited state, with the mean space falling from 40.2 to 39.2 options and the verified arms’ masked accuracy moving by at most 0.1 points; of those 307 out-of-space targets, 274 are SOC-service names and 33 are tool names outside the catalog), an arithmetic upper bound no readout inside the declared space can exceed—we report accuracy both overall and within the declared space. The carve is deterministic and trace-disjoint: every trace hashes to train/validation/test at 70/10/20 (first 8 hex digits of its sha256, mod 100), so every train-versus-held-out claim below except the E4 gate comparisons refers to episodes whose traces no fit saw (the self-evolution stream’s finer split of the validation fold is decision-row-granular: rows, not traces, are split, a leakage risk disclosed here and now measured—re-cutting the stream and the gate at whole-trace granularity moves held-out accuracy by under 0.1 points and leaves every E4 conclusion in place).

Baselines and arms.

E2 compares a per-node majority arm (raw per-node argmax) against multinomial logistic regression and typed readouts trained on one observable-state feature set (node, goal, prefix statistics, visit counters, per-node neighbor statistics); the typed readouts are trained with cross-entropy versus the CE-plus-Brier variant (5 training seeds each); in the edge-ID variant the readout space is the induced graph’s edge identifiers rather than target-action classes. Two class-space readouts use Laya: zero-shot typed choice over each state’s declared options, and a frozen-encoder hidden-state probe—a linear head on the encoder’s designated readout position—trained with the same CE and CE-plus-Brier objectives. E3 compares: a re-prompted MIMO Pro V2.6 stand-in over the reconstructed state (MIMO Pro V2.6, a production reasoning model at our serving gateway—one call per decision, without the fleet’s per-stage orchestration and without tool results—not the deployment’s status quo) deciding every hop from the same reconstructed state and options (under the richer full-label prompt rendering of the replay protocol); typed readouts acting greedily within the masked option set; and typed with accept/escalate at τ∈{0.55,0.75,0.9}\tau\in\{0.55,0.75,0.9\}, which routes low-confidence states to MIMO Pro V2.6. Readouts are named after their table rows: feature MLP scores engine-derived stream statistics, hidden-state probe is a probe fit on Laya’s frozen hidden states, and typed encoder is the Laya backbone itself scoring the declared options.

Metrics and protocol.

Per decision: top-1 agreement with the logged hop, masked-renormalized over the declared options for the trained arms, reported overall and within the declared space (for the baseline rows the displayed cells are raw top-1; their option-masked variant merely gates the raw argmax on landing in the option set—no renormalization); calibration (ECE-15, per the §4 convention; it is computed on the 3,568 in-space rows for the zero-shot arm—a typed-choice head gives no score to an out-of-space target—and on all 3,875 rows with out-of-space targets counted wrong for the other arms, whose full-vocabulary heads still define a masked-renorm confidence there). Risk–coverage curves (Geifman & El-Yaniv, 2017) and the area under the risk–coverage curve (AURC) for the accept/escalate gate complete the per-decision set. Per episode: strict survival (no divergence before the log ends), LLM calls per decision, and the wrong-hop gap accumulated over the whole teacher-forced episode under both per-hop cost conventions (1 and 3). Difficulty profile: domain (agent-stage) slices and local branch-factor buckets (≤\leq3, 4–10, 11+: the train-graph out-degree at the current node, stop options excluded). Uncertainty: 5 training seeds for the readout arms (mean ±\pm std); the E3 replay and the E4 refit chain are single-seed (seed 0) sequences (E4’s ten-chain stress study is aggregated at the unit of one refit chain: 30.3% and 31.0% are across-chain means of start and end held-out accuracy, ±0.5\pm 0.5 points—one standard deviation across the ten chains’ end accuracies); service and judge latencies are in-vivo wall-clock (p50/p90), the zero-shot arm’s runtime in-vivo CPU (App. B), typed-model timings batch-1 GPU wall clock (App. B). Each of E1–E4 is annotated with the claim it tests.

6 Results

E1: the induced action graph’s node vocabulary converges (its edge set runs a long tail; claim P1).

Figure 3 provides quantified saturation curves on real production traces, adding the transition-pair long tail and the loop-event mass to the usual state-count view. Across 20 without-replacement subsamples per size (medians quoted here and in Figure 3), the semantic node vocabulary saturates fast: 77 action labels appear in 50-episode subsamples, 124 at 400, 142 at 1,000, against 154 in the full corpus. Transition discovery is the honest counterpoint—observed transition pairs keep a long tail (336 at 50 episodes →\to 1,267 at 400 →\to 2,027 at 1,000 →\to 2,536 at 1,615), and the recovery side never closes either: 702 pairs appear at recovery returns, 481 of them doubling as forward transfers in other contexts (§3). Loop mass is heavy and stable: 29.2% of executed steps fold into loop events (4,124 retry—63.6% of loop events, in 2,164 bursts—and 2,364 back returns—36.4%, 146 per 100 episodes; revisit distances concentrate at 1–3 steps behind the current frame, with 681 taking the immediate-repeat distance of one). Two consequences: the router’s label space closes early—the stability pattern of Cho et al. (2026) recurs in the node curve (qualitatively, a small saturating node set of 77 to 154 labels rather than their 7–43 states; Figure 3a), now alongside the transition-pair and loop-mass axes—while per-node option sets keep thickening. The routing task on real traces is therefore bounded-vocabulary but long-tailed option selection: exactly the regime where a masked, calibrated typed readout constrains the damage of open-vocabulary guessing.

E2: the router reaches top-1 agreement with the fleet (32.8%) and decides in milliseconds (claim P2).

Table 3 replaces the ordering reading with paired tests on the same held-out states and 95% intervals from 2,000 trace-clustered bootstrap resamples over the 345 test episodes (resampling decisions independently would understate the interval: dependence inside an episode is strong). Two of the six comparisons separate—the readout against the per-node majority arm (+5.7+5.7 points, CI [+4.6,+6.9][+4.6,+6.9]) and the edge-ID collapse on the hidden-state probe (−3.8-3.8 points, CI [−5.0,−2.6][-5.0,-2.6])—while the CE/CE++Brier ordering, the feature MLP against logistic regression, and the edge-ID penalty on the feature arms all have intervals that include zero and are therefore reported as point estimates. Table 4 gives the branch-factor view: the headline accuracy is a weighted average dominated by the 11+11+ bucket (89.6% of rows), the ≤3\leq 3 bucket is effectively solved (92%92\% majority, 99%99\% in-space for the best arm), and the small middle bucket is the hardest in-space case. Finally, the information budget behind these numbers is small: once node identity and the eight state statistics are given, adding seven prefix-latency features buys +0.4+0.4 points and adding argument-shape counts on top of them +1.3+1.3 points (five seeds, feat_lat_results.json, Reproducibility), so the ordering among feature arms should not be read as evidence that richer signals were the missing ingredient.

Table 2 states the difficulty plainly: next-hop prediction on production traces tops out at 32.8% agreement on the state features (feature MLP, CE; 35.6% within the declared space) with its CE-plus-Brier twin at 32.7%, the logistic-regression arm at 32.3% (raw top-1) and the majority arm at 26.8%. These absolute levels measure the task as much as the models: the reference behavior is a realized fleet policy rather than a planner oracle, states offer 40.2 declared options on average (median 46, stop included), and 7.9% of targets fall outside the train-declared option space (a 92.1% declared-space arithmetic upper bound, 91.3% under prefix-marked reachability, for masked readouts; that restriction shifts the feature-MLP and edge-ID arms by at most 0.00050.0005 accuracy and leaves 29 of 3,875 rows without their target, so no reported level depends on it). Three structural findings hold on production traces. At this catalog size semantic class sharing beats structural book-keeping: the class-space readout beats the edge-ID readout on shallow features (32.7% versus 31.6% masked; both CE++Brier, 5 seeds) and by far on the hidden-state probe (30.7% versus 26.6%; the edge-ID probe’s ECE explodes to 0.458)—the reverse of our design bet, discussed in §9. Also, the CE-plus-Brier objective pays where the readout trails and is flat where it already leads (the probe trails here and gains; the feature leads and is flat): on the feature MLP it gives up 0.05 accuracy points and worsens ECE by 0.002 versus plain CE (32.7% versus 32.8%, ECE 0.048 versus 0.045, deltas on unrounded 5-seed means), while on the hidden-state probe it adds 0.4 points (30.3% →\to 30.7%) and cuts the seed spread (±0.007\pm 0.007 →\to ±0.004\pm 0.004). And the designated-position hidden-state readout of Cheng et al. (2026) is its system’s answer path and wins system-level comparisons; here, encoder held fixed, the structured feature arm beats the designated hidden-position probe (32.7% versus 30.7%; in-space 35.5% versus 33.3%). For a proprietary 154-name catalog described by name only, the structured feature arm wins this comparison (although representation, readout family and training budget are confounded here: the features summarize the folded kept prefix while the probe’s state text renders raw logged labels through the name-tail surface of §5 and trails the current label wherever retries precede it, by up to dozens of raw steps; the probe reads through a linear head on encoder state where the feature arm is an MLP over the observable features; and the probe’s reported fit runs 90 epochs against the feature arm’s 60). Zero-shot typed choice (8.6% overall, 9.3% within the declared space; fitted temperature T=3.0T{=}3.0, the ceiling of an eight-point refit grid T∈{0.5,0.7,1.0,1.3,1.6,2.0,2.5,3.0}T\in\{0.5,0.7,1.0,1.3,1.6,2.0,2.5,3.0\} and still the ceiling when the grid is extended to T=1000T{=}1000: the raw head is over-confident and the fit is unbounded (validation NLL falls monotonically to the uniform-prediction limit 3.403.40; the argmax is invariant, the risk–coverage curve moves by at most 0.00060.0006, and ECE-15 is grid-dependent—0.0310.031 at T=3.0T{=}3.0 against 0.0100.010 at T=1000T{=}1000—so this arm’s calibration is not to be read as calibrated confidence) shows what transfer alone buys. Calibration is another honest limit: the probe’s ECE sits at 0.122 against 0.045 for the best feature arm, and confidence on the feature arms stratifies sharply only at the top of its ranking—selective risk on features falls to 3% at 5% coverage and 23% at the top quartile (the seed-0 dense curve; full risk–coverage curves in Figure 4), then rises more slowly (48% at 50% coverage to 67% at full coverage on the feature MLP with CE++Brier, five-seed means; 52% →\to 69% at the same two anchors on the hidden-state probe with CE++Brier). The accept/escalate gate therefore lives or dies with the hybrid sweep in E3. Where the data are easy the readout is easy: the hidden-state probe’s branch-factor and domain-slice refits (60-epoch fits over its frozen encoder features, App. B; real/e8_slices.json) answer the 263 test states in the ≤\leq3 local-branch-factor bucket at 92.2% (aggregated over 5 seeds ×\times the test split), 21.2% on the 139 states in the 4–10 bucket, and 25.9% on the 3,473 states in the 11+ bucket—the middle bucket dips below the largest. By domain slice the same probe refits average 28.9% (detection), 41.9% (response), 29.3% (protection) and 42.2% (recognition)—an ordering §9 cautions against reading directly, since stage accuracy conflates routing with pipeline role (closure rates in App. A).

E3: end-to-end replay against the re-prompted MIMO Pro V2.6 stand-in (claim P3).

Table 5 delivers the end-to-end outcome (Figure 5). With all 3,875 decisions of the 345 held-out episodes scored against the fleet’s own behavior, the re-prompted MIMO Pro V2.6 stand-in (one reasoning call per hop; its free-text replies are matched to option names post hoc, 66 replies—1.7%—unparsed and scored as divergences) agrees with the reference at 9.6%; the hidden-state probe holds 30.7% at zero LLM calls; and the accept/escalate hybrids land below the typed layer—20.9% / 19.1% / 16.5% at τ∈{0.55,0.75,0.9}\tau\in\{0.55,0.75,0.9\} under escalation rates of 74.1% / 80.2% / 85.0% (MIMO Pro V2.6 consulted on the readout’s least-confident states; the τ\tau sweep traces the agreement/cost curve that slopes down). The episode-level measures agree with the per-decision read: strict survival keeps 2 of 345 episodes for the hidden-state probe (0.6%) and none for the opponent or the hybrids—any-divergence death on ten-plus-hop episodes asks for perfection in every hop—while the wrong-hop gap charges 10.2 wrong hops per episode against the opponent (30.5 under c3c_{3}) and 7.8 (23.4) for the hidden-state probe. The hybrids land at 8.9/9.1/9.4 (26.7/27.3/28.1 under c3c_{3}). The cost asymmetry holds regardless of who wins the agreement column: every typed decision is one bounded readout pass—a typed-choice predict at 19.5 ms p50 with the encoder pass included (17 declared options measured, below the 40.2-option held-out mean), or, on the replay’s probe rows, that pass alone (10 ms) plus a linear head (App. B)—while every MIMO Pro V2.6 decision is a reasoning generation at 2.2 s p50 (7.4 s p90) under the serving configuration’s 2,048-token completion budget. We account for cost on the three axes the export actually carries—decision latency, LLM calls per decision, and the wrong-hop cost of a divergence—and not in tokens or currency: the stripped stream we work from records no per-call usage, so a token-level comparison here would be modelled, not measured. Two readings follow. Matching this fleet is hard for everyone—the reference is a realized multi-agent policy whose tool results our export strips (§9)—and within that hard task the cheap readout beats the zero-shot opponent outright, 3.2×3.2\times its agreement at two orders of magnitude less decision time. This comparison is asymmetric in construction: the readout is fit on 12,613 logged reference decisions while the stand-in is only ever re-prompted zero-shot with tool results stripped (66 of its replies, 1.7%, fail to parse into a valid tool choice and score 0 against the fleet’s logged next hop), so 9.6% is a transfer-floor number for a stripped stand-in, not the deployed component’s own capability ceiling. Tuning is the difference: jpt-4b, LoRA-tuned for one epoch on the training fold, reaches 31.9% against the typed encoder’s 32.2% on the same held-out decisions, a gap an exact paired test does not resolve (p=0.68p=0.68, 229 decisions the tuned model gets and the typed encoder misses, 239 the other way), at 244 ms per decision against 10 ms (Table 13). The hybrid result is a negative one for confidence-gated cascade calibration on this stream. The gate routes roughly four of every five hops to the LLM (3.7–4.3 of every five hops at 74.1/80.2/85.0% for the three τ\tau thresholds) and inherits the opponent’s low agreement on those hops, so rather than beating both parents on their complementary states it sits strictly between its parents—an escalation rule needs per-state competence, not just confidence, before it can pay for itself here.

Threshold scale, and where routes first diverge.

The raw thresholds above are not scale-free: pmaxp_{\max} lives on a per-node simplex whose dimension is the option count, and the threshold that matches a given escalation rate correlates with 1/|A⁡(v)|1/|A(v)| at Pearson r=0.52r=0.52. Re-running the sweep on an excess-over-uniform scale, an entropy-normalized scale, the top-1/top-2 margin, and a threshold-free rule that escalates the least-confident fraction, at matched escalation rates, leaves the reading unchanged: at 74.1% escalation the hybrid reaches 0.2085 (raw) / 0.2263 (excess over uniform) / 0.2098 (entropy-normalized) / 0.2101 (margin) / 0.2085 (rank only) against 0.3061 for the pure hidden-state-probe row, so the cascade’s loss is not an artifact of an uncalibrated threshold and no tested scale closes more than 1.8 of the 9.8-point gap. Where a route dies is a quantity the per-decision mismatches do not carry: of the 343 episodes that diverge at all under the hidden-state probe, 60 diverge at the first hop and 185 at the second (median 2)—routes are lost on the way in; 331 of those first divergences sit at states with 11+11+ declared options, 12 at out-of-space targets, and 258 fall on hops the hybrid had escalated.

E4: the gated loop absorbs the corruption stress on average, and the rollback gate is exercised—13 of 40 candidate updates refused over ten seeded chains (claim P3).

Across four rounds (Figure 6) the gated loop accumulates the self-evolution stream in 300-decision batches—each candidate is a refit of the hidden-state probe on accumulated data (train split plus accepted batches). The stress arrives at round 3 (12% of the batch’s labels flipped to uniformly drawn non-target options, App. A): against a 12,613-decision base the injected flips do not dent held-out accuracy—the five fits run 30.2% →\to 30.4% →\to 30.4% →\to 31.0% →\to 31.7% on the untouched test split with the gate score rising alongside (25.0% →\to 27.1%)—and every refit, corrupted one included, is committed (5 fits on the chain, base plus four refits; 4 of 4 candidate updates accepted; 0 reverts at δ=0.005\delta{=}0.005). What the run demonstrates is monotone accumulation and noise absorption at this injection rate, not a gate rescue: a stress sized to bite was run as that honest next test, and the answer is partly negative. At 30% and 50% (four chains each, same recipe, injection still in round 3) the gate refuses 7 and 8 of 16 candidate updates against 8 at 12% while the corrupted update’s gate score falls further (0.00130.0013 and 0.00590.0059 mean drop against 0.00070.0007 at 12%), and final held-out accuracy stays within 0.0020.002 of the base (31.2%31.2\% and 30.9%30.9\% against 30.8%30.8\%)—so the refusal path is exercised at every rate but neither the refusal count nor the held-out metric tracks the injection size, because the 0.50.5-point threshold already separates the same updates. The other half of that test—corruption against a smaller base—was run too: at a quarter of the base (3,1533{,}153 decisions) the fit starts 2.62.6 points lower (27.6%27.6\% against 30.3%30.3\%), the gated loop recovers most of the gap over the four updates (29.5%29.5\% and 29.6%29.6\% against 30.8%30.8\% and 31.3%31.3\%), and the rollback path fires on every chain (3/2/13/2/1 refusals at 12% and 3/0/13/0/1 at 30%), including the chain that never fires at the full base—so base size, not injection size, is what makes the gate bite. Direction check at the same 12% rate: a second batch replaces the observation instead—the feature row shown to the model is taken from another stream row with a different logged target, the label left intact—and is absorbed the same way (6 rollbacks across the same five runs against 7; final held-out accuracy 31.08% against 31.05%), so the loop’s behaviour here does not depend on which side of the imitation pair is corrupted, and the gate is not a mislabel-specific detector. Richer world- and harness-evolution loops are complementary (Xue et al., 2026; Zheng et al., 2026; NeoHorse Team et al., 2026).

Ablations (A1–A3).

(A1) Without loop folding the readout would face the raw stream of 22,192 positions of which 29.2% are loop bookkeeping: folding removes only the 4,124 retries (18,068 decision states remain: 15,704 forward plus 2,364 recovery returns—the same accounting E5’s 237-kept-frame example spells out) and compresses the state-ID space to 154 semantic labels (Figure 3a). (A2) CE++Brier training is flat against plain CE on the class-space readout (paired Δ=−0.13\Delta=-0.13 points, 95% trace-clustered CI [−0.53,+0.26][-0.53,+0.26]: an unresolved ordering, not a win; Table 3) and nudges the edge-ID readout up a notch (31.4% →\to 31.6%, ECE 0.082 →\to 0.080); it buys its margin on the hidden-state probe (the E2 deltas, tabulated in Table 6): a hedge for whichever readout trails rather than free accuracy. (A3) The accept/escalate sweep lives in the hybrid rows of Table 5 (escalation rate is monotone in τ\tau by construction) and in the risk–coverage curves of Figure 4; the deployed gate thresholds the masked-renormalized distribution, and out-of-space emissions are masked back into range (§5).

E5: external replication on public corpora (generalization probe).

Does the loop-collapsed action-graph picture survive outside security operations? Following the process-mining methodology of van der Aalst (2016), we run the identical fold over six public process-mining and software-engineering event logs (saturation curves over the five that support subsampling)—loan applications (BPIC’12 and BPIC’17 from the BPI Challenge series van Dongen, 2012; van Dongen, 2017, each log’s fetch host and sha256 pinned in App. B), permit applications and service desks (receipt Buijs, 2014, helpdesk Polato, 2017), traffic-fine handling (roadtraffic de Leoni & Mannhardt, 2015) and one instrumented software-tool session (statechart Leemans, 2018): 60,613 cases and 1,549,559 events in total (Table 7; URLs, sha256 provenance and a builder-correction ledger in App. B). Two findings generalize (i–ii); the third (iii) probes the catalog-size boundary condition. (i) Loop mass is corpus-generic and often larger than the SOC corpus’s 29.2%: 59.2% on BPIC’12 (immediate repeats alone are 105,776 of 262,200 events) and 59.3% on BPIC’17 (448,205 retries and 264,654 back returns inside 1,202,267 events), against 8.9% (helpdesk), 2.9% (receipt) and 1.4% (roadtraffic). The instrumented software session is the extreme case: 17,675 of its 17,912 events are immediate repeats and another 131 are back returns (99.4% loop mass counting both event kinds)—the fold compresses the session’s 17,912-event stream into 237 kept frames (106 first-visit advances plus 131 returns). (ii) Graph growth saturates decisively in nodes (Figure 7): distinct-node discovery flattens near the catalog ceiling wherever the vocabulary is small, while forward-pair (E+E^{+}) discovery keeps a long tail to the case boundary—the E1 node-vocabulary convergence is not SOC-specific. The dashed occupancy null (Figure 7 caption) matches every observed median to a mean absolute deviation of 0.2–1.0 nodes on the five process logs (0.2–1.2 nodes with the SOC stream, Figure 3, as a sixth, undrawn point: 1.2 of its 154 nodes, 0.78% of that catalog; normalized deviations run 0.78%–4.06% across the six streams): for node discovery, conditional on the observed label supports, saturation is combinatorics rather than a lucky property of one deployment. (iii) The same held-out decision construction (recipe unchanged; option and edge vocabularies rebuilt per corpus from its training fold) carries to open tool-use trajectories: 26,999 ToolBench multi-step chains (Qin et al., 2023) over a 7,318-name API catalog (47.5×47.5\times the SOC’s 154 names), the large-catalog regime where the edge-ID variant (§9) is hypothesized to pay. API-Bank—a 50-name nested-call set at the other end of the catalog scale—adds 261 loaded dialogues from 263 scenario files (Li et al., 2023) (its 335-row training fold fell below the catalog-size sweep’s training floor). The sweep results for the ToolBench catalog are summarized in App. B.

Beyond these corpus findings comes the readout-level decomposition. The majority arm claims 26.8% on the SOC stream but jumps to 66.3% on BPIC’17 and to 87.2% on helpdesk, where that stream’s feature MLP (87.3% masked) sits inside half a point of its own majority baseline—once the majority arm itself runs this high, the readout has little left to add. Margins over the majority arm vary sharply by stream—+6.0 points on SOC (the feature-MLP CE arm: 32.8% masked against 26.8%), +22.7 on BPIC’17 (the feature-MLP CE arm: 89.0% masked against 66.3%), +26.4 on BPIC’12 (the feature-MLP CE++Brier arm: 80.8% masked against 54.4%)—reported here descriptively. A variable-order Markov baseline with backoff-style interpolation (the backoff Markov; the standard prefix-scoring baseline of predictive process monitoring; App. B) probes how much of each margin is memorizable transition structure: contexts over the traced node flow (the last 0–3 nodes of history; order counts context nodes, so the order-3 table conditions on a 3-node history—a 4-gram counting its target) are counted, orders interpolated to the marginal, and the table option-gated like the deployed masked-renorm gate. On the five process logs (BPIC’12, BPIC’17, helpdesk, receipt, roadtraffic) the order-3 table (each log’s per-stream best) collects most of each margin (within ±2.5\pm 2.5 points): 89.7% on BPIC’17 against the feature MLP’s 89.0%, and 83.9% on receipt against the feature MLP’s 86.4% (CE++Brier; its majority arm 75.1%). On the two large agent streams—SOC and the 7,318-name ToolBench training catalog—transition tables fall short of the readout: the best order-kk table stops at 31.1%, short of the feature MLP’s 32.8% on SOC, and at 7,318 names no order-kk table even reaches the 37.6% majority arm that the CE++Brier arm beats by 3.2 points. The featurized residual (MLP minus the table’s per-stream best) is within ±2.5\pm 2.5 points across the five process logs and positive at the point estimate on both large agent streams—a comparison whose caveats run to the table’s benefit (order chosen as its per-stream best on the same test split; moving the choice to the validation fold, which every public stream already carries, leaves the picture unchanged: validation picks the same order on six of the nine streams, and on the other three it picks one whose test accuracy is at or below the test-selected order’s (largest gap 0.6 points, ToolBench evaluation), so the validation-selected column never flatters the table; the public folds are already session-isolated—0 of 17,942 test traces appear in training, and a trace-disjoint refit reproduces every order’s accuracy exactly; point estimates, no intervals). The residual, rather than the raw margin over the majority arm, is what the feature MLP adds beyond order-≤\leq3 backoff transition tables—a residual that is conservative under the on-test order selection above—not beyond stream statistics at large (the feature MLP’s own inputs are stream statistics). ToolBench-eval (the 351-name evaluation subset, 161 hops) and API-Bank sit at the hard end and motivate the cautions below. There the ToolBench runs reproduce the SOC’s masked-below-declared direction, with a gap far wider than the SOC’s own (32.8% masked versus 35.6% within the declared space, the CE arm): 34.9% masked against 66.9% within the declared option space (CE++Brier arm) on the 351-name evaluation subset (47.8% of test targets leave the declared options), and 40.8% against 48.2% on the 7,318-name training catalog (CE++Brier; 15.4% out-of-space). Four cautions accompany the comparison. (i) The majority arm (37.6%) edges the multinomial logistic-regression arm (35.7% masked, 36.4% raw) at 7,318 classes (an 800-iteration budget under-converges a linear arm at this scale). (ii) The small nested-call set reverses the logistic/MLP order (API-Bank: logistic 61.5% versus the feature MLP’s 56.9% on the CE++Brier arm; the stream’s interpolated tables reach 59.6%—above the feature MLP and the majority arm but below the logistic arm). (iii) On the same set the edge-ID readout leads the class-space readout (59.0% versus 55.6% masked, both CE arms). (iv) On the 351-name evaluation subset (161 held-out hops) the order-2 table (a 2-node history—the 3-gram) leads (36.0% masked/69.0% in-space versus the class-space readout’s 34.9%/66.9%). The controlled catalog-size sweep in App. B tracks which of these effects moves with catalog size (narrower budgets also carry narrower train/test splits here).

E9: what the induced graph is worth (necessity ablation).

The probe arm reads only the frozen encoder state, so on that arm the induced graph enters solely through the declared option space A⁡(v)A(v). Holding features, readout (linear probe), recipe, seeds and budget fixed and changing only the evaluation-time option space, the declared space reaches 30.67% while a flat 155-class catalog reaches 27.07% (−3.5-3.5 points), a size-matched global train-frequency space 29.60% (−1.4-1.4), and a random KK-set 8.4% (Table 8); a re-implementation of the published probe reproduces the frozen headline to four decimals (30.67% mean masked agreement against 30.67%; per-seed spread 0.0037 against 0.0039), so the arms are comparable. A node-conditioned space that uses the same node identity but no graph traversal reaches 30.79% (+0.1+0.1 points; paired trace-clustered bootstrap CI [0.0,+0.3][0.0,+0.3] over 2,000 resamples; 6 wins, 1 loss, 3,868 ties), and the union of targets ever observed at that node gives the same number. The additivity is the reading we claim: flat →\to size-matched frequency prior +2.5+2.5 points, frequency prior →\to node conditioning +1.2+1.2, node conditioning →\to graph traversal ≈0\approx 0. Two limits on that reading: the arm is the probe, not the feature MLP (where the graph additionally enters through engineered node features), and the node-conditioned competitor uses the targets observed at the node, which is close to the graph’s own outgoing-edge set (mean 40.4 vs. 40.2 options); what the ablation separates is therefore node identity from graph traversal, not node information from none. Artifacts are listed in the Reproducibility section.

7 What the typed interface can replace, and what it cannot

Earlier sections score one realised next hop. This section asks a narrower question with a deployment consequence. Which part of that decision can a small trained model take over, and which part needs an agent that can see more of the episode than the released state exposes? Every number below is read from the held-out fold or from an arm we ran for this section, and each table names the artefact its columns come from.

E23a: scale does not move the zero-shot reading.

jpt-4b, a 4B general-purpose checkpoint asked to choose among the declared options, reaches 9.0% agreement (9.9% within the declared space) on a seeded 200-decision sample. On the typed model’s twenty-candidate shortlist it reaches 9.5%, or 10.5% in space (Tables 9 and 13). The domain encoder reaches 8.6% zero-shot on the full fold. The diagnostic is less flattering. Its accuracy equals the sample’s majority-class rate, and it picks the candidate printed first 22% of the time against a 5% uniform rate. Order was shuffled per decision, so the bias cannot pass for competence. On the same 200 decisions the fine-tuned encoder reaches 31.0%. Tuning is what separates the two families here, so Table 13 adds the tuned reading on the full fold.

E23b: fine-tuning moves it, and fine-tuning is what moves it.

Freezing the encoder and training the decision head alone gives 27.7% (30.1% in space). Unfreezing the encoder for three epochs gives 32.2% (34.9%). The 4.5-point difference is attributable. The two arms share the renderer, the option set, the optimiser and the epoch budget, and differ only in which parameters receive gradients. The gradient path is the whole effect. The fine-tuned arm sits 0.65 points below the strongest feature readout in Table 2 (32.8% and 35.6%). The typed interface reaches parity with the hand-built feature arm. Three numbers of similar size appear in this paper from three protocols rather than one quantity. 32.8% is the strongest hand-built feature readout, 32.2% the fine-tuned typed encoder measured here, and 32.15% a full-supervision run under the loop protocol of Section 8. All three score the same frozen held-out fold.

E23c: narrowing the option set does not substitute for state.

The fine-tuned model ranks the realised next hop inside its top twenty for 90.7% of the fold. Narrowing the candidate set does not hand the decision to a general model. On a random 800-decision subset jpt-4b scores 9.9% over all declared options, 12.1% over twenty candidates and 19.9% over five, while the typed encoder reaches 32.2% over all options on the full fold (Tables 9 and 13). A shortlist that contains the answer almost nine times in ten does not let a zero-shot general model find it. Tuning the same checkpoint on the same protocol and fold closes almost all of that gap. It reaches 31.9% against the typed encoder’s 32.2% on the full held-out fold, a difference of 0.25 points. An exact paired test over the same 3,875 decisions does not resolve it: 229 decisions the tuned model gets and the typed encoder misses, 239 the other way, p=0.68p=0.68. On the shared 800 decisions its agreement rises from 9.9% to 33.0% (p<10−3p<10^{-3}). What the typed encoder keeps is cost, 10 ms against 0.24 s per decision, and a tenfold smaller parameter count. The accuracy advantage over a language model belongs to tuning, not to the interface. What binds is the state text, not the number of candidates.

E23d: task intent helps by about one point; more context does not help at all.

Three arms share one training recipe, one seed and one batch size, and differ only in the state string (Table 10). Adding the decision’s own goal field, a six-valued enum, lifts agreement by 1.08 points, from 32.00% to 33.08%. Replacing the eight-action window with the full action prefix, while keeping the goal, drops it by 1.39 points. Length is not the lever. The released records carry the goal field and the published renderer never exposes it, so this increment is available today at no extra cost. Both increments are single-run point estimates from one harness at one seed, and the 1.08-point gain sits inside the 1.9-point cross-run spread reported in Section 8. The larger claim, that a plan or playbook in the state would lift the in-graph decision far higher, is the interface change this paper cannot yet measure.

E23e: the released state carries a measurable ceiling.

To bound what any state-conditioned predictor can reach here, we grouped held-out decisions by an increasingly specific key (Table 11). Each group kept only decisions from other traces, and we asked how often a decision agrees with the modal choice of its group. The construction is leave-one-out and cross-trace, so a trace never votes for itself. The reading rises with the key and then flattens: 25.6% for the station alone, 26.5% with one preceding action, 38.6% with three, 42.8% with the full released prefix. Requiring at least two other-trace observations raises the last figure to 44.9%, but over a shrinking support: the group behind 25.6% holds all 3,857 decisions, while the group behind 44.9% holds only the 1,234 (31.8%) whose key recurs in another trace, and the levels are therefore not scored over a common denominator. With everything the release exposes, repeated states still disagree more often than they agree. Agreement with a single realised sample cannot approach one on this fixture. No confidence rule can lift the accepted subset to 90% at any coverage, and no model size changes that: the constraint is the state, not the capacity.

E23f: two questions, two operating points.

Containment and agreement must not be conflated. For containment the shortlist reaches 90.7% at twenty candidates. The residual 9.3% needs an agent holding the full episode. The share of held-out targets that fall outside the declared options altogether is 7.9%. Both figures sit under the 20% escalation budget a deployed cascade can afford. For agreement, we sorted decisions by top-1 probability and kept the most confident subset (Table 12, Figure 8). Accepted accuracy holds above 90% up to 15% coverage, 91.9% at 15%, 82.2% at 20%, 37.7% at 80%. A confidence gate therefore buys a small high-precision band. The band is not an artefact of the score: at 15% coverage, margin gives 89.2% and negative entropy 91.9%. The trained encoder answers the containment question; the ceiling above bounds the agreement question.

E23g: agreement tracks task outcome, modestly.

Readouts in Table 2 are scored against the fleet’s realised choices. We also asked what those choices predict. Over the 345 held-out traces, a median split on agreement gives 68.8% completion in the upper half against 62.2% in the lower half. Completed traces are longer, at 15.5 steps against 10.3, so we repeated the split inside step-count strata. The gap sits in mid-length traces: +46.0 points at 6–10 steps, separating 22.2% completion from 68.3% over 126 traces, against +2.0 at 2–5, +12.5 at 11–20 and +22.4 at 21 or more, where both halves clear 70%. This is an association. A mechanism would need a controlled rollout, and the labels are model-derived.

8 What a gated loop adds over full supervision

Section 7 bounded a single decision. The deployment question is whether a loop can raise that bound on its own, by turning the graph’s own unlabelled traffic into training rows. This section runs the loop and reports what it does, including where it fails.

E25a: protocol.

We split the training fold by trace into an anchor set of 3,071 decisions and an unlabelled pool of 9,542, and froze the test fold. Each round draws 600 pool rows, admits some of them by the arm’s own rule, retrains the typed encoder for two epochs on the buffer and re-scores the frozen fold. The gate sees no label for the row it admits. It compares the current model’s argmax against a variable-order backoff table built only from buffer rows and admits the row when the two agree. A random arm admits a fixed number of rows per round, and a third arm runs the same accounting with no typed model at all, using that variable-order backoff table itself as the predictor, a Markov-style control (Table 14).

E25b: the loop moves, and it stops below supervised training.

Every typed arm ends above its own anchor-only starting point. The peaks come before the last round: at seed 0 the gate peaks at 30.48% in round 4 and ends at 28.80%, averaging 29.39% over three seeds. The induced graph grows from 1,015 to 1,257 edges (Figure 9). Full supervised training on the same fold reaches 32.15%. No arm closes that gap. The high-precision band also stays at half its width: accepted accuracy holds above 90% up to 6.8% of coverage under the gate, against 15% for the fully trained head. The loop is a real but limited mechanism here. What it cannot do is manufacture the information the state lacks.

E25c: controls.

Two controls bound the reading. First, selection. Each arm draws its own anchor set, so round-0 scores spread over 1.9 points (26.45% to 28.31%) across the seven runs we have; seed 0 alone gave 0.8 points. That spread is our noise floor. At matched admitted volume the gate averages 29.39% over three seeds (28.80, 29.37, 29.99). Random admission averages 28.77% (27.56, 29.45, 29.29). The per-seed gaps are +1.24+1.24, −0.08-0.08 and +0.70+0.70 points, a mean of +0.62+0.62. A sign test over the three paired seeds gives two positives and one negative (p=1.0p=1.0). The gap therefore sits inside the floor, and at this scale the gate’s advantage over volume-matched random admission is inside seed noise. We report the gap as a point estimate with its seed range. The unrestricted random arm admits 43% more rows and lands 0.49 points above the gate at seed 0 (one run). More unselected data thus roughly compensates for worse selection. Selection quality is a weak effect at this scale. Acquisition volume is the stronger term. Second, capacity. With no typed model the same accounting reaches 25.91%, which is 2 to 3 points below the typed arms. Its 90%-accuracy band collapses to 0.001. The typed encoder is what makes an accept-or-escalate band exist at all.

E25d: what grows, and what that does not show.

Edge counts rise in every arm, but they track how much of the pool an arm consumed: the model-free arm consumes the most and finds the most edges. Growth of the graph is therefore evidence that the loop explores, not that the gate selects well. Combining the two sections, the honest summary of the deployment claim is this. The typed interface replaces the per-decision deliberation with a millisecond forward pass and reaches parity with the strongest feature readout, containment is 90.7% at twenty candidates, and escalation needs to cover under 10% of decisions. Raising in-graph accuracy past a third of the fold is not a matter of more self-training, more parameters or more deliberation. It needs a state that carries the plan and the observation, which the released records do not.

E25e: what a deployment should do with this.

Three operating points follow from the two sections, and they are meant to be read together. Inside the graph, route with the typed encoder and accept its decision: one forward pass, no generated text, 19.5 ms per decision in the typed-choice form and 10 ms for the encoder pass the replay uses. At the top of the confidence ranking, accept a band rather than the whole fold: 15% coverage holds 91.9% agreement. Return the rest, because the realised hop lies outside the declared options for 7.9% of decisions and outside the model’s top twenty for 9.3%, so a budget under 20% covers both measures. Returning a decision is escalation, and its price is measured: on the replay stream the accept/escalate hybrids agree with the reference on 20.9% / 19.1% / 16.5% of decisions at escalation rates of 74.1% / 80.2% / 85.0% (Table 5), below the pure readout’s 30.7% at zero calls, and the escalated remainder costs 2.2 s a decision, so an 85% budget moves mean decision time from 2.2 s to about 1.9 s. The band is a latency and load instrument rather than an agreement gain, and it assumes an escalation arm stronger than the zero-shot stand-in these hybrids were measured against. Above that budget none of the remedies tested here applies: more self-training, more parameters and more deliberation each leave the ceiling where the state puts it. The escalation rule itself must carry per-state competence rather than confidence alone, since the confidence-gated cascade lost agreement at every threshold we tested.

9 Limitations and Discussion

Replay evaluation. The held-out logs are a realized environment, not a live one: policies are scored against the deployed fleet’s own choices (teacher-forced scoring, strict survival and per-wrong-hop gap costs), so a policy that would improve on the reference cannot demonstrate that improvement here—agreement with the fleet at a fraction of its decision cost is the claim. Closed-loop rollouts with tool results reattached (this needs a fuller export than the stripped one described here) are the natural next step. The graph-free comparison that scores every catalog action as one flat option space is run here (E9, Reproducibility): the flat catalog loses 3.5 points and a size-matched global-frequency space loses 1.4 points, so restricting candidates per node is load-bearing, but a node-conditioned space built from per-node train statistics without graph traversal matches the graph-declared space within noise (+0.1+0.1 points, 95% trace-clustered CI [0.0,+0.3][0.0,+0.3]). The induced graph’s measured value here is therefore as a construction that yields node-conditioned option sets, not as a traversal whose specificity this data can resolve. Derived labels. Task outcomes come from the close-out convention (§5): the convention is machine-checkable and checked against an assistant’s manual session-log re-reading (30/30), but it certifies declared completion, not the semantic quality of the report text—which the export strips. The unconstrained-judge failure mode we quantify (38.5% agreement when the judge expects report text in a field that never carries it) is a caution for LLM-judge pipelines generally: calibrate against a manual session-log re-reading, not against another judge. Scope of the claims. We evaluate a decision layer over logs that already exist. Authorization, retention and re-identification boundaries of the underlying sessions, the human review roles around them, change management for catalog updates, and the explicability a planner needs when it cannot verify its own outputs are properties of the deployment that produced the logs; we do not measure them, and our audit statements are limited to what the export can show (which, as noted above, includes no separate human auditor in the loop). State reconstruction. Tool result bodies and chat bodies are absent from the export (the tool-result field is null in all 22,192 tool records; call arguments survive, below), so the router’s context is structural (labels, ordering). Two result-adjacent families do survive in the export and go unused in the main pipeline—per-call latency (100% of tool calls) and the call arguments (98.9%)—so their contribution is already measurable without the payloads: an artifact-shape-verified reproduction of the §6 feature-MLP CE++Brier arm scores 32.7% masked agreement, and appending prefix-latency / latency-plus-argument-shape features adds +0.4 / +1.3 points (five seeds, feat_lat_results.json, Reproducibility)—a small but real measured gain that stops this limitation’s prediction being an untested assertion. Domains and slices. One security-operations deployment, four stage slices; the protection-stage zero close-out rate (App. A) means slice comparisons conflate routing behavior with pipeline role. Edge IDs. The per-edge identifiers do not beat the class-space readout at the SOC catalog size with our shallow state features—the small API-Bank set and the 351-name ToolBench-eval subset are the material small-catalog reversals (§6, Figure 10)—and the natural counter—that verdict being a small-catalog artifact—is now tested: a controlled catalog-size sweep on the 7,318-name ToolBench catalog (Figure 10, App. B) holds recipe and features fixed while shrinking the option vocabulary to the top-CC actions by train frequency (CC, the kept catalog budget). The row-filtered sweep gives a class advantage of net +0.9 points at C=154C{=}154 to +1.3 at C=6,750C{=}6{,}750 (a dip to +0.6 at C=512C{=}512).
